title: Environmental variation and extra-pair paternity in birds: a global comparative meta-analysis
text:
Environmental variation and extra-pair paternity in birds
    A reproducible workflow for a global comparative meta-analysis
    
      
        Author
        Aneta Arct, Santiago Ortega, Agnieszka Gudowska, Karolina Skorb, Monika Gronowska, Magdalena Zagalska-Neubauer, Dorota Kotowska, Szymon M. Drobniak, Malgorzata Lagisz, Shinichi Nakagawa
      
      
        Last rendered
        August 19, 2026
      
    
  
  
    
  




This book documents a reproducible comparative analysis of environmental variation and extra-pair paternity (EPP) in birds. The analysis uses population-level estimates of the proportion of sampled broods containing at least one extra-pair young and links them to environmental conditions, geography, species identity, phylogeny, and sampling structure.



The project is organised around three primary mean-only environmental model groups: an environmental PCA model, a short-anomaly model, and a long-anomaly model. All three use a beta-binomial response and include methodological controls for nest-box use and genetic marker type. Their exploratory location-scale extensions are presented separately so that effects on mean EPP and effects on residual dispersion are not conflated.



The book also reports the preregistered direct-predictor and zero-inflated specifications, temperature-anomaly interactions with latitude, within- versus between-population anomaly effects, within-season climatic variability, absolute-anomaly sensitivity models, and a contextual comparison with Botero and Rubenstein (2012). These analyses are retained as separate chapters so that registered tests, confirmatory extensions, and exploratory sensitivity analyses remain distinguishable.




  Main question
  Do population-level EPP rates vary along broad environmental gradients related to temperature, precipitation, thermal variability, productivity, latitude, and distance to coast? Do year-specific temperature and precipitation departures from local short- and long-term norms predict EPP, and do temperature-anomaly associations differ across latitude or within versus among populations?


Website structure



  
    
      1.
      Environmental data sources
      
        Description of the climate, productivity, and geographic datasets used to characterise breeding-season environmental conditions.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      2.
      Data preparation
      
        Construction of the analytical dataset linking EPP records to sampling effort, breeding timing, location, and environmental predictors.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      3.
      Taxonomy and phylogeny
      
        Taxonomic harmonisation and preparation of the phylogenetic covariance matrix used in the comparative models.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      4.
      Overall model structure
      
        Beta-binomial response structure, priors, random effects, methodological controls, sampler settings, inference rules, and the baseline variance decomposition.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      5.
      Environmental PCA
      
        Six correlated environmental-geographic predictors are summarised into a thermal-geographic axis and a wet-productivity axis, with the retained-component decision documented explicitly.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      6.
      Main environmental mean models
      
        Three main model groups are fitted:
      
      
        Environmental PCA model (PC1 + PC2)
        Short anomaly model
        Long anomaly model
      
      
        These are the primary mean-only models: predictors enter the expected EPP component while beta-binomial precision is global. Exploratory location-scale extensions are reported in Chapter 15.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      7.
      Registered direct-predictor model
      
        The preregistered specification enters temperature, precipitation, DTR, NDVI, latitude, and distance to coast directly. Because these predictors are strongly collinear, the PCA model is reported as primary and this registered model assesses sensitivity to that choice.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      8.
      Temperature anomaly × latitude
      
        Confirmatory interaction models test whether short- and long-term temperature-anomaly associations become more negative with increasing absolute latitude, with explicit low-latitude support checks.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      9.
      Within- and between-population anomaly effects
      
        Temperature anomalies are decomposed into population means and within-population departures to distinguish spatial differences among populations from temporal change within the same population.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      10.
      Seasonal temperature variability
      
        A supplementary model tests whether persistent within-year temperature variability, calculated from CRU TS v4.09, is associated with EPP in the population-year dataset.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      11.
      Comparison with Botero & Rubenstein
      
        Contextual comparison with the 2012 species-level analysis, including the 44-of-122 species overlap, validation of the PGLS pipeline against the published coefficient, Bayesian population-level tests, and the latitude-adjusted model.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      12.
      Preregistered zero-inflated models
      
        The preregistered zero-inflated beta-binomial family is tested directly. The structural-zero probability is approximately 0.0056, the standard model already reproduces zero counts, and exact-reloo comparisons favour the simpler beta-binomial model.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      13.
      Within-season climatic variability
      
        The preregistered H1 model evaluates breeding-season temperature and precipitation means together with their month-to-month variability on the corrected 422-record model frame.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      14.
      Absolute climate-anomaly sensitivity
      
        Sensitivity models test anomaly magnitude irrespective of sign, complementing the signed-anomaly models used for the primary directional hypotheses.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      15.
      Exploratory location-scale models
      
        Separate exploratory models allow environmental and methodological predictors to enter the beta-binomial precision component and ask whether residual dispersion changes systematically.
      
    
    
      Open chapter
    
  

  
    
      16.
      Figures
      
        Final figures, model summaries, and visual outputs used to interpret environmental effects and present the main results.
      
    
    
      Open chapter

The analyses reported in this project can be reproduced from the processed files included in the repository. Full re-extraction of environmental variables requires the CRU archives identified in the checked manifest and the Google Earth Engine products used for NDVI extraction. The large CRU NetCDF archives are not redistributed in this repository.






WarningRaw-climate provenance limitation



The original repository contained the derived CRU columns but did not contain the post-1990 monthly NetCDF inputs, the original extraction script, or the original locality-to-cell lookup. It was therefore not self-contained at the raw-climate level. CRU TS v4.09 and the used grid cells were identified later by exact empirical reconstruction of the stored values. This demonstrates a reproducible source for the columns, but it is a forensic reconstruction rather than proof that the original raw artifacts or extraction log were preserved.

title: 1  Environmental data sources
section: 1.4 CRU TS product, years, and grid-cell provenance
text:
1.4 CRU TS product, years, and grid-cell provenance
The temperature (tmp), precipitation (pre), and diurnal temperature range (dtr) variables in the analysis-ready data were extracted from CRU TS v4.09, a monthly gridded product at 0.5-degree resolution. The exact official archive release is cruts.2503051245.v4.09; the CRU TS v4.09 archive and variable-specific directories for temperature, precipitation, and diurnal temperature range are publicly accessible. CRU describes the product and its 0.5-degree monthly grid on its high-resolution climate-data page. The product should be cited as Harris et al. (2020), doi:10.1038/s41597-020-0453-3.
The actual study-year range used by tmp_cru_C_first_month, pre_cru_mm_first_month, and dtr_cru_C_first_month in the 441-record main model frame is 1982–2018; all three variables are complete over this range. It is not a 1901–2018 extraction. The reconstruction therefore reads the 1981–1990, 1991–2000, 2001–2010, and 2011–2020 archives, with 414 records occurring after 1990. Temperature and precipitation archives for 1961–1980 are additionally required only to calculate the 1961–1989 long baseline and the earliest rolling five-year baselines. These files were absent from the audited repository. The newly checked manifest identifies 16 required archives totalling 701,912,161 bytes (approximately 0.65 GiB) and records every official URL, byte size, and SHA-256 checksum.
The raw inputs can now be reobtained reproducibly, but they are still not committed to Git because of their size:
python scripts/download_cru_ts_v409.py
The downloader stores them under data_raw/cru_ts_4.09/, verifies both byte count and SHA-256 before reporting success, and refuses to replace an existing nonmatching file unless --force is supplied explicitly.
The original locality-to-cell lookup file was not retained. We therefore recovered the used grid cell empirically for each of 162 unique coordinates by comparing the stored first-month temperature and precipitation series with candidate CRU land cells within 100 km. Candidate cells were ranked first by the number of failures against the 0.01-degree-C/0.1-mm tolerances, then by scaled reconstruction error, and finally by distance. The selected cell reproduces all stored first-month values. Distance is the Haversine great-circle distance from the reported locality coordinates to the centre of the assigned 0.5-degree CRU grid cell, using an Earth radius of 6,371.0088 km. The recovered map is saved rather than recomputed during subsequent extraction. This step matters at coordinates lying exactly on a 0.5-degree cell boundary and at coastal localities, where a generic nearest-cell rule need not select the original land cell.

All 441 first-month values and all 426 available full-season values were reproduced to floating-point precision. This includes every one of the 414 post-1990 records. No reconstructed value differed by more than 0.001, and none crossed the prespecified hard thresholds of 0.01 degrees C for temperature/DTR or 0.1 mm for precipitation. The earlier failed within-season check used CRU TS v4.10 and an approximate grid lookup; it was a product-version and cell-mapping mismatch, not evidence that the post-1990 climate values lacked a source.
For a breeding window wholly within a calendar year, temperature and DTR are means across the named months and precipitation is their sum. For the 63 complete windows whose reported start month is later than the end month (for example, October–January), the historically stored full-season fields retained all named months under the record’s single climate_year: October–December and January were read from that same calendar year. Those fields and the corresponding same-year H1 fit are retained only as a provenance audit. In the final preregistered H1 analysis, the full-season means and within-season standard deviations were re-extracted from CRU TS v4.09 using the corrected calendar convention: months through December use climate_year, and January-side months use climate_year + 1. The product and recovered grid-cell mapping were first validated on 22 non-cross-year records from 1982–1990, with maximum absolute differences of \(4.0\times10^{-9}\) degrees C and \(4.8\times10^{-8}\) mm. This correction affects only full-season variables and H1; the main climate and anomaly models use the first breeding month and therefore require no refitting.

title: 1  Environmental data sources
section: 1.5 NOAA NDVI products and extraction scale
text:
1.5 NOAA NDVI products and extraction scale
The Earth Engine script in ndvi_extraction/EPP_NDVI_NOAA_AVHRR_VIIRS_median_30x30km_first_full_records.js uses two daily NOAA Climate Data Record products:

NOAA Climate Data Record (CDR) of AVHRR Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Version 5, Earth Engine collection NOAA/CDR/AVHRR/NDVI/V5 and NOAA dataset doi:10.7289/V5ZG6QH9. The Earth Engine collection covers 24 June 1981 through 31 December 2013. It supplies 399 final-model records dated 1982–2013.
NOAA Climate Data Record (CDR) of VIIRS Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Version 1, Earth Engine collection NOAA/CDR/VIIRS/NDVI/V1 and NOAA dataset doi:10.25921/gakh-st76. The collection begins on 1 January 2014 and is continuing; it supplies the 42 final-model records dated 2014–2018.

Both products provide daily NDVI on the same 0.05-degree by 0.05-degree global grid. Earth Engine reports a nominal band pixel size of 5,566 m. Throughout this project, a pixel means one native 0.05-degree NOAA CDR grid cell at this nominal scale. It does not mean a native 375-m or 750-m VIIRS sensor observation, and it does not mean the complete 30-by-30-km extraction window. Because the source grid is geographic, 0.05 degrees is the defining spatial resolution and the physical east–west width of a grid cell decreases with latitude.
The script masks daily cells flagged as cloud, cloud shadow, water, sunglint, night, or invalid channel data and applies the catalog scale factor of 0.0001. For each record it constructs a square extending 15 km from the study coordinate in each direction. It then calculates the temporal median of valid daily NDVI separately for every native product pixel over the first breeding month or complete breeding window, followed by the arithmetic mean of those pixel-level medians across the 30-by-30-km square using scale = 5566. Consequently, despite the historical column names, ndvi_first_month_median_30km and ndvi_full_season_median_30km are temporal-pixel medians followed by a spatial mean; they are not spatial medians of the 30-km window.

1.5.1 NDVI missingness and spatial selectivity
Among the 571 response-complete records considered for the common environmental model frame, first-month NDVI was unavailable for 111. The extraction audit separated these cases without an unresolved remainder: 60 records could not be submitted with the required inputs because coordinates or the first breeding month were missing, while 51 had complete inputs but returned a null NDVI value because no valid pixel remained in the 30-by-30-km window after quality masking. The latter category is important because water, cloud, shadow, sunglint, night, and invalid-channel masks do not remove study systems at random.
At the species level, the complete-case restriction reduced the dataset from 153 to 110 Clements species. Thirty-three of these 43 lost species had no usable NDVI record: 17 lacked extraction inputs for every record, 15 returned no valid pixel for every record, and one had both failure mechanisms across its records. The other 10 species had at least one NDVI value and were removed by another model-frame requirement. Nine of the 15 species lost entirely after NDVI masking belonged to unequivocal seabird families; the masked set also included island and high-latitude populations. Consequently, the environmental models under-represent marine, island, and polar study systems. This is a limitation on their ecological scope of inference, not only a loss of sample size. Record- and species-level classifications are retained in ndvi_missingness_audit.csv and ndvi_species_loss_audit.csv.
The loss was also phylogenetically structured at the order level, rather than being dispersed evenly across the avian tree. Among Clements species, Suliformes declined from six represented species before environmental complete-case filtering to none in the final 441-record frame, Procellariiformes from nine to three, and Sphenisciformes from six to two. Thus, one order was removed completely and two marine orders lost most of their representation. This structural thinning is relevant to interpretation of the phylogenetic variance component and strengthens the limitation on inference to marine and polar lineages.

title: 1  Environmental data sources
text:
1.7 Climate-anomaly sign and time windows
Climate anomalies are stored as signed differences: the CRU value in the study year minus the corresponding local baseline, never as an absolute deviation. For climate variable \(x\), locality \(i\), breeding month or window \(m\), and study year \(y\),
\[
A^{\mathrm{short}}_{i,m,y}=x_{i,m,y}-\frac{1}{5}\sum_{t=y-5}^{y-1}x_{i,m,t},
\]
and
\[
A^{\mathrm{long}}_{i,m,y}=x_{i,m,y}-\frac{1}{29}\sum_{t=1961}^{1989}x_{i,m,t}.
\]
Thus positive temperature anomalies denote warmer conditions and positive precipitation anomalies wetter conditions than the relevant local baseline. The primary anomaly models use only the first reported breeding-season month. A direct CRU TS v4.09 reconstruction reproduced every stored short- and long-baseline value and every signed anomaly for all 441 first-month records (and all 426 available full-season records), with no absolute difference greater than 0.001. Exact definitions, sign interpretation, standardization, and the independent algebraic identity check are also given in Section 6.2.

title: 2  Data preparation
text:
2.1 Overview
This chapter documents the preparation of the analytical dataset used in the analyses. The workflow starts from the analysis input file, checks the response variables, restricts the data to socially monogamous species, defines population-level identifiers, and summarises the final dataset used in the Bayesian models.
The legacy database of Brouwer and Griffith contained 488 unique publications. Of these, 286 publications (58.6%) were excluded because their EPP estimates could not be assigned to individual study years, leaving 202 publications (41.4%) with annual-resolution EPP data. Results of the literature update for studies published after 1 August 2017, including the number contributing eligible year-specific EPP data, are reported separately in the PRISMA flow diagram. Throughout this chapter, study counts refer to unique publications (id_reference), species counts use Clements v2025 names, and repeated population-year observations are not counted as separate studies.

2.3 Clements v2025 taxonomic corrections
Scientific names were checked against the Clements Checklist v2025 before the publication-overlap rule was applied. The former broad Yellow Warbler concept (Dendroica petechia, later Setophaga petechia) was split in Clements v2025. The reviewed northern breeding populations in this dataset were therefore assigned to Setophaga aestiva; the name Setophaga petechia is now restricted to Mangrove Yellow Warbler. The correction is accepted only after the target species and split text are found in the local Clements v2025 file. title: 2  Data preparation
text:
2.4 Publication-overlap resolution
To prevent repeated use of the same population-years across publications, records were compared using the Clements-matched species name (Clements_name), study year, and geographic coordinates. Two publication series were treated as potentially overlapping when they represented the same Clements species, shared at least one study year, and their reported locations were no more than 25 km apart. Within every such comparison, the publication series covering the longest temporal span was retained and the shorter series was removed in full, including its non-overlapping years. This prevents a shorter report derived from the same study system from contributing additional weight beside a longer report. Exact repeated biological results within the same publication were reduced to one record before the between-publication comparison.
When temporal spans were equal, ties were resolved reproducibly using, in order, the number of observed years, the total number of sampled broods, the number of records, and the reference identifier. The rule was applied to all species before restricting the dataset by breeding system. No record was removed solely because two studies were geographically close: an overlapping study year was also required.

title: 2  Data preparation
text:
2.8 Breeding system restriction
The main analyses are restricted to socially monogamous species. This restriction is important because EPP is defined relative to social pair bonds. EPP estimates are therefore not directly comparable across systems without stable social pair bonds, or across polyandrous, lekking, or non-pair-bonded mating systems.
After resolving duplicate and overlapping publication series, the combined annual dataset contained 237 unique publications representing 167 species. The breeding-system restriction excluded 14 publications representing 13 species: 13 publications inherited from the Brouwer and Griffith database and one publication identified in the literature update. Twelve species were removed from the analysis entirely; one additional species, the Aquatic Warbler (Acrocephalus paludicola), also had a retained publication classified as socially monogamous. The socially monogamous dataset therefore contained 223 unique publications representing 155 species. These counts are publication- and species-level totals, not counts of annual records.

2.9 Response variable checks
The response variable is the number of broods with EPP out of the total number of broods sampled. Records were retained for modelling only when brood counts were available, the total number of sampled broods was greater than zero, and the number of EPP broods did not exceed the total number of sampled broods.

  summarise(
    n_records = n(),
    missing_epp_broods = sum(is.na(n_epp_broods)),
    missing_total_broods = sum(is.na(n_broods_sampled)),
    missing_both_response_counts = sum(is.na(n_epp_broods) & is.na(n_broods_sampled)),
    missing_epp_only = sum(is.na(n_epp_broods) & !is.na(n_broods_sampled)),
    missing_total_only = sum(!is.na(n_epp_broods) & is.na(n_broods_sampled)),
    zero_total_broods = sum(n_broods_sampled == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    epp_greater_than_total = sum(n_epp_broods > n_broods_sampled, na.rm = TRUE),
    records_excluded_response_qc = sum(
      is.na(n_epp_broods) |
        is.na(n_broods_sampled) |
        n_broods_sampled <= 0 |
        n_epp_broods > n_broods_sampled,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )

title: 2  Data preparation
text:
2.12 Environmental predictor complete-case restriction
The response-complete dataset is broader than the common frame used by the main environmental models. The model-fitting script additionally requires complete first-month climate and NDVI values, geographic covariates, anomaly variables, categorical moderators, and phylogenetic identifiers. The following audit names this previously implicit filtering step and separates missing NDVI caused by unavailable extraction inputs from null Earth Engine results after quality masking.


Show code
main_environmental_frame <- readRDS(
  "models/main_environmental_models/dat_main_environmental_models.rds"
)
ndvi_input <- read_csv_safe(
  "ndvi_extraction/EPP_NDVI_GEE_input_all_records.csv",
  na = c("", "NA", "NaN")
)
ndvi_output <- read_csv_safe(
  "ndvi_extraction/EPP_NOAA_NDVI_median_30x30km_first_full.csv",
  na = c("", "NA", "NaN")
)

if (anyDuplicated(dat_model$record_id) ||
    anyDuplicated(ndvi_input$record_id) ||
    anyDuplicated(ndvi_output$record_id)) {
  stop("NDVI missingness audit requires unique record_id values.")
}

ndvi_input_match <- match(dat_model$record_id, ndvi_input$record_id)
ndvi_output_match <- match(dat_model$record_id, ndvi_output$record_id)
if (anyNA(ndvi_input_match)) {
  stop("Some response-complete records are absent from the Earth Engine input table.")
}

ndvi_missingness_audit <- dat_model %>%
  transmute(
    record_id,
    Clements_name,
    family,
    lat,
    long,
    climate_year,
    breeding_start_month_num,
    breeding_end_month_num,
    stored_ndvi = ndvi_first_month_median_30km,
    can_first_month = ndvi_input$can_first_month[ndvi_input_match],
    gee_output_present = !is.na(ndvi_output_match),
    gee_output_ndvi = ndvi_output$ndvi_first_month_median_30km[ndvi_output_match]
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    missing_coordinates = is.na(lat) | is.na(long),
    missing_study_year = is.na(climate_year),
    missing_start_month = is.na(breeding_start_month_num),
    missing_required_input = missing_coordinates |
      missing_study_year | missing_start_month,
    missing_stored_ndvi = is.na(stored_ndvi),
    no_valid_pixel_after_masking = can_first_month == 1 &
      gee_output_present & is.na(gee_output_ndvi),
    missingness_category = case_when(
      !missing_stored_ndvi ~ "NDVI available",
      missing_required_input | can_first_month == 0 ~
        "Missing coordinates, study year, or first breeding month",
      no_valid_pixel_after_masking ~ "No valid pixel after masking",
      TRUE ~ "Unresolved"
    )
  )

ndvi_missingness_summary <- ndvi_missingness_audit %>%
  count(missingness_category, name = "n_records") %>%
  mutate(percent_of_571 = 100 * n_records / nrow(dat_model))

if (sum(ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_stored_ndvi) != 111L ||
    sum(ndvi_missingness_audit$missingness_category ==
          "Missing coordinates, study year, or first breeding month") != 60L ||
    sum(ndvi_missingness_audit$missingness_category ==
          "No valid pixel after masking") != 51L ||
    any(ndvi_missingness_audit$missingness_category == "Unresolved")) {
  stop("NDVI missingness reconciliation failed: expected 111 = 60 + 51 records.")
}

ndvi_input_missingness <- tibble(
  input_problem = c(
    "Missing coordinates (including overlap with missing month)",
    "Missing first breeding month (including overlap with coordinates)",
    "Missing study year",
    "Coordinates only",
    "First breeding month only",
    "Both coordinates and first breeding month"
  ),
  n_records = c(
    sum(ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_stored_ndvi &
          ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_coordinates),
    sum(ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_stored_ndvi &
          ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_start_month),
    sum(ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_stored_ndvi &
          ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_study_year),
    sum(ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_stored_ndvi &
          ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_coordinates &
          !ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_start_month),
    sum(ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_stored_ndvi &
          !ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_coordinates &
          ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_start_month),
    sum(ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_stored_ndvi &
          ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_coordinates &
          ndvi_missingness_audit$missing_start_month)
  )
)

environmental_filter_funnel <- tibble(
  stage = c(
    "Response-complete socially monogamous dataset",
    "Common main-environmental-model frame"
  ),
  n_records = c(nrow(dat_model), nrow(main_environmental_frame)),
  n_populations = c(
    n_distinct(dat_model$population_id),
    n_distinct(main_environmental_frame$population_id)
  ),
  n_clements_species = c(
    count_clements_species(dat_model),
    count_clements_species(main_environmental_frame)
  )
)

lost_clements_species <- setdiff(
  unique(as.character(dat_model$Clements_name)),
  unique(as.character(main_environmental_frame$Clements_name))
)

ndvi_species_loss_audit <- ndvi_missingness_audit %>%
  filter(Clements_name %in% lost_clements_species) %>%
  group_by(Clements_name, family) %>%
  summarise(
    n_records = n(),
    any_ndvi_available = any(!missing_stored_ndvi),
    all_missing_input = all(
      missingness_category ==
        "Missing coordinates, study year, or first breeding month"
    ),
    all_masked = all(missingness_category == "No valid pixel after masking"),
    no_ndvi_available = all(missing_stored_ndvi),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    species_loss_category = case_when(
      any_ndvi_available ~
        "At least one NDVI value available; removed by another requirement",
      all_missing_input ~ "All records lack coordinates or season date",
      all_masked ~ "All records have no valid pixel after masking",
      no_ndvi_available ~ "Mixed NDVI failure mechanisms",
      TRUE ~ "Unresolved"
    )
  )

species_loss_summary <- ndvi_species_loss_audit %>%
  count(species_loss_category, name = "n_clements_species")

if (length(lost_clements_species) != 43L ||
    sum(ndvi_species_loss_audit$all_missing_input) != 17L ||
    sum(ndvi_species_loss_audit$all_masked) != 15L ||
    sum(ndvi_species_loss_audit$species_loss_category ==
          "Mixed NDVI failure mechanisms") != 1L ||
    sum(ndvi_species_loss_audit$any_ndvi_available) != 10L) {
  stop("Species-loss reconciliation failed: expected 43 = 17 + 15 + 1 + 10 species.")
}

seabird_families <- c(
  "Alcidae", "Diomedeidae", "Fregatidae", "Procellariidae",
  "Spheniscidae", "Stercorariidae", "Sulidae"
)
masked_records <- ndvi_missingness_audit %>%
  filter(missingness_category == "No valid pixel after masking")
masked_lost_species <- ndvi_species_loss_audit %>%
  filter(all_masked)

masked_epp_records <- dat_model %>%
  semi_join(masked_records %>% select(record_id), by = "record_id")

summarise_raw_epp <- function(data, group) {
  tibble(
    group = group,
    n_records = nrow(data),
    n_clements_species = n_distinct(data$Clements_name),
    n_broods = sum(data$n_broods_sampled),
    n_epp_broods = sum(data$n_epp_broods),
    pooled_raw_epp_percent =
      100 * sum(data$n_epp_broods) / sum(data$n_broods_sampled),
    mean_record_epp_percent =
      100 * mean(data$n_epp_broods / data$n_broods_sampled)
  )
}

masked_raw_epp_summary <- bind_rows(
  summarise_raw_epp(main_environmental_frame, "Retained environmental model frame"),
  summarise_raw_epp(masked_epp_records, "No valid NDVI pixel after masking"),
  summarise_raw_epp(
    masked_epp_records %>% filter(family %in% seabird_families),
    "Masked records: strict seabird families"
  ),
  summarise_raw_epp(
    masked_epp_records %>% filter(!family %in% seabird_families),
    "Masked records: other families"
  )
)

masked_seabird_orders <- masked_epp_records %>%
  filter(family %in% seabird_families) %>%
  group_by(order) %>%
  summarise(
    n_masked_records = n(),
    n_masked_species = n_distinct(Clements_name),
    families = paste(sort(unique(family)), collapse = ", "),
    n_broods = sum(n_broods_sampled),
    pooled_raw_epp_percent = 100 * sum(n_epp_broods) / sum(n_broods_sampled),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

eligible_order_coverage <- dat_model %>%
  filter(order %in% masked_seabird_orders$order) %>%
  group_by(order) %>%
  summarise(
    eligible_records = n(),
    eligible_species = n_distinct(Clements_name),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

retained_order_coverage <- main_environmental_frame %>%
  filter(order %in% masked_seabird_orders$order) %>%
  group_by(order) %>%
  summarise(
    retained_records = n(),
    retained_species = n_distinct(Clements_name),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

masked_seabird_order_coverage <- masked_seabird_orders %>%
  left_join(eligible_order_coverage, by = "order") %>%
  left_join(retained_order_coverage, by = "order") %>%
  mutate(
    retained_records = coalesce(retained_records, 0L),
    retained_species = coalesce(retained_species, 0L),
    order_lost_entirely = retained_records == 0L
  ) %>%
  select(
    order, families, n_masked_records, n_masked_species,
    eligible_species, retained_species, order_lost_entirely,
    n_broods, pooled_raw_epp_percent
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_masked_records), order)

orders_lost_entirely <- setdiff(
  unique(as.character(dat_model$order)),
  unique(as.character(main_environmental_frame$order))
)

if (nrow(masked_epp_records) != 51L ||
    sum(masked_epp_records$family %in% seabird_families) != 18L ||
    !setequal(orders_lost_entirely, c("Ciconiiformes", "Suliformes"))) {
  stop("Taxonomic/EPP audit of masked NDVI records did not reproduce expected totals.")
}

write_csv_safe(
  ndvi_missingness_audit,
  "data/processed/ndvi_missingness_audit.csv"
)
write_csv_safe(
  ndvi_species_loss_audit,
  "data/processed/ndvi_species_loss_audit.csv"
)

This restriction removed 130 records, 59 populations, and 43 Clements species. NDVI was missing for 111 of the 571 candidate records. The causes were fully reconciled: 60 records lacked coordinates or the first breeding month needed to request an Earth Engine extraction, whereas 51 had complete inputs but no valid pixel remained in the 30-by-30-km window after masking. No study year was missing. Among the 60 input-limited records, 3 lacked coordinates only, 47 lacked the first breeding month only, and 10 lacked both.

At the species level, 33 of the 43 lost species had no usable NDVI record: all records of 17 species lacked coordinates or a season date, all records of 15 species returned no valid pixel after masking, and one species had both failure mechanisms across its records. The remaining 10 lost species had at least one NDVI value and disappeared because of another complete-case requirement.
The masking failure was taxonomically and ecologically selective rather than a simple random loss. Eighteen of the 51 masked records (35.3%) belonged to seven unequivocal seabird families, and 9 of the 15 species lost entirely through masking (60.0%) were seabirds. The affected set also included island and high-latitude populations. This reflects the combined water, cloud, shadow, sunglint, night, and invalid-channel masks and means that the final environmental frame under-represents marine, island, and polar study systems. It is therefore a limitation on the ecological scope of inference, not merely a reduction in sample size.
The selection was also associated with the response. Pooling brood counts, the 51 masked records had 16.8% EPP, compared with 33.0% in the retained 441-record frame. This difference was concentrated in the 18 records from strict seabird families (10.5%); the other 33 masked records had 31.4%. These are unadjusted descriptive rates and remain confounded by species and study composition, but they show that environmental complete-case filtering was associated with both phylogeny and the observed outcome.

The 18 conservatively classified seabird records belonged to four orders. The loss was not limited to isolated tips of the phylogeny: all six eligible Suliformes species were absent from the retained frame. Procellariiformes declined from nine to three species and Sphenisciformes from six to two, while Charadriiformes retained eight of 14 species. Across the entire 571-to-441 restriction, two orders disappeared completely: Suliformes (six species) and Ciconiiformes (one species). The Ciconiiformes loss was a single record from a single species, White Stork (Ciconia ciconia), and is therefore not comparable in scale with the loss of all six represented Suliformes species. The direction of the marine selection was also informative: the 18 masked records from strict seabird families had pooled raw EPP of 10.5%, compared with 33.0% in the retained frame, and they occupied a small number of phylogenetically distinct marine clades. Their omission removes low-EPP between-clade extremes and is therefore expected to bias the estimated phylogenetic variance downward. The reported phylogenetic variance should consequently be regarded as conservative for the eligible dataset, while still not being extrapolated directly to the omitted marine lineages.

title: 2  Data preparation
text:
2.13 Reference-population overlap
The overlap between reference identity (id_reference) and population identity (population_id) is checked directly from the response-complete dataset. This summary was used to evaluate whether reference identity and population identity represented sufficiently distinct grouping structures.


Show code
if (file.exists("data/processed/dat_model.rds")) {
  overlap_dat <- readRDS("data/processed/dat_model.rds")
} else {
  overlap_dat <- read_csv_safe("epp_data_June2026.csv") %>%
    mutate(
      lat_round = round(as.numeric(lat), 2),
      long_round = round(as.numeric(long), 2),
      population_id = paste(Clements_name, lat_round, long_round, sep = "_")
    )
}

overlap_dat <- overlap_dat %>%
  mutate(
    id_reference = if ("id_reference" %in% names(.)) {
      as.character(id_reference)
    } else {
      as.character(id)
    }
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    population_id = as.character(population_id)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(id_reference), !is.na(population_id))

population_overlap <- overlap_dat %>%
  group_by(population_id) %>%
  summarise(
    n_records = n(),
    n_references = n_distinct(id_reference),
    id_references = paste(sort(unique(id_reference)), collapse = "; "),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

reference_overlap <- overlap_dat %>%
  group_by(id_reference) %>%
  summarise(
    n_records = n(),
    n_populations = n_distinct(population_id),
    .groups = "drop"
  )




Show code
population_overlap %>%
  count(n_references, name = "n_populations") %>%
  mutate(percent_populations = 100 * n_populations / sum(n_populations)) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

In this dataset, 223 of 230 populations (96.96%) are represented by a single publication, and only 7 populations occur in more than one publication. The study and population groupings are therefore almost completely nested on the population side, making separate study- and population-level random-intercept variances weakly identifiable. We retained the population random intercept because population is the repeated-observation unit and because it also links the few populations reported in multiple publications. Omitting the preregistered study-level random intercept is a deviation from the registered model specification; this overlap diagnostic and its rationale are reported here for the Supplementary Methods under “Reference-population overlap.”

title: 2  Data preparation
text:
2.14 Environmental window correlations
The main environmental models use environmental values from the first breeding-season month. As a data check, we compared these values with the corresponding full-season summaries for temperature, precipitation, diurnal temperature range, and NDVI. The CRU full-season summaries used here follow the corrected calendar convention: for seasons crossing a year boundary, months through December use climate_year and January-side months use climate_year + 1. NDVI already used this continuous-season convention.


Show code
corrected_fullseason_climate <- read_csv_safe(
  "models/withinseason_models_corrected/withinseason_climate_by_record.csv",
  na = c("", "NA", "NaN")
)

required_corrected_columns <- c(
  "epp_row_id", "crosses_year_boundary",
  "recomputed_tmp_cru_C_full_season",
  "recomputed_pre_cru_mm_full_season",
  "recomputed_dtr_cru_C_full_season"
)
missing_corrected_columns <- setdiff(
  required_corrected_columns,
  names(corrected_fullseason_climate)
)
if (length(missing_corrected_columns)) {
  stop(
    "Corrected full-season climate audit is missing: ",
    paste(missing_corrected_columns, collapse = ", ")
  )
}

environment_window_data <- main_environmental_frame %>%
  mutate(epp_row_id = as.character(epp_row_id)) %>%
  left_join(
    corrected_fullseason_climate %>%
      transmute(
        epp_row_id = as.character(epp_row_id),
        crosses_year_boundary =
          tolower(as.character(crosses_year_boundary)) == "true",
        tmp_cru_C_full_season_corrected =
          as.numeric(recomputed_tmp_cru_C_full_season),
        pre_cru_mm_full_season_corrected =
          as.numeric(recomputed_pre_cru_mm_full_season),
        dtr_cru_C_full_season_corrected =
          as.numeric(recomputed_dtr_cru_C_full_season)
      ),
    by = "epp_row_id",
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  )

if (nrow(environment_window_data) != 441L ||
    sum(environment_window_data$crosses_year_boundary %in% TRUE, na.rm = TRUE) != 63L) {
  stop("Corrected environmental-window audit did not reproduce 441 records and 63 cross-year seasons.")
}

environment_window_pairs <- tribble(
  ~variable, ~first_month, ~full_season,
  "Temperature", "tmp_cru_C_first_month", "tmp_cru_C_full_season_corrected",
  "Precipitation", "pre_cru_mm_first_month", "pre_cru_mm_full_season_corrected",
  "DTR", "dtr_cru_C_first_month", "dtr_cru_C_full_season_corrected",
  "NDVI", "ndvi_first_month_median_30km", "ndvi_full_season_median_30km"
)

environment_window_correlations <- purrr::pmap_dfr(
  environment_window_pairs,
  function(variable, first_month, full_season) {
    keep <- complete.cases(environment_window_data[, c(first_month, full_season)])
    test <- cor.test(
      environment_window_data[[first_month]][keep],
      environment_window_data[[full_season]][keep],
      method = "pearson"
    )

    tibble(
      variable = variable,
      n_complete = sum(keep),
      pearson_r = unname(test$estimate),
      lower_95_ci = test$conf.int[1],
      upper_95_ci = test$conf.int[2]
    )
  }
)

write_csv_safe(
  environment_window_correlations,
  "models/climate_provenance/corrected_environment_window_correlations.csv"
)

environment_window_correlations %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  knitr::kable()

After assigning January-side CRU months to the following calendar year for all 63 cross-year seasons, the correspondence between first-month and full-season values was high for temperature (r = 0.910), DTR (r = 0.919), and NDVI (r = 0.799), but only moderate for precipitation (r = 0.498). These correlations are calculated on the 441-record main environmental frame using the corrected CRU TS v4.09 full-season fields; pair-specific sample sizes are reported in the table. The two temporal windows should therefore not be regarded as interchangeable for precipitation: precipitation coefficients in the main models describe conditions in the first breeding-season month and should be interpreted with this limitation. The preregistered analysis specified environmental aggregation across the complete breeding window; using first-month predictors in the main models is a deviation from that specification and is documented here for the Supplementary Methods.

title: 3  Taxonomy and phylogeny
text:
3.1 Overview
This chapter prepares the taxonomic and phylogenetic structure used in the Bayesian comparative analyses. Starting from the cleaned modelling dataset created in the data-preparation chapter, species names are linked to a Clements-matched avian phylogeny, the tree is pruned to the retained species, and a phylogenetic correlation matrix is generated for use in brms.

title: 3  Taxonomy and phylogeny
text:
3.9 Prepare phylogenetic grouping variables
Two species-level grouping variables were retained for the Bayesian models:

species_phylo - species identity linked to the phylogenetic covariance matrix;
species_nonphylo - species identity modelled as an additional non-phylogenetic random effect.

Including both random effects allows the models to partition variation attributable to shared evolutionary history and species-specific variation not explained by phylogeny.

title: 4  Overall model structure
text:
4.1 Overview
This chapter defines the common statistical structure used across the Bayesian models. It describes the beta-binomial response model, the population, species, and phylogenetic grouping terms used for the expected EPP probability, and the distinction between mean-only and location-scale models. Reference identity (id_reference) is not included as a separate grouping term: in the 571-record response-complete dataset, 223 of 230 populations (96.96%) were represented by a single publication. Population identity therefore captures nearly all of the repeated-observation structure available on the population side, while including both study- and population-level random intercepts would make their variances weakly identifiable. This omission of the preregistered study effect and its empirical justification are reported explicitly in the data-preparation chapter.

library(dplyr)

title: 4  Overall model structure
text:
4.2 Response model
For record \(i\), the response is the number of sampled broods with EPP:
\[y_i = \texttt{n\_epp\_broods}_i,\]
out of the total number of sampled broods:
\[n_i = \texttt{n\_broods\_sampled}_i.\]
The model likelihood is:
\[y_i \sim \operatorname{BetaBinomial}(n_i, \mu_i, \phi_i),\]
where \(\mu_i\) is the expected EPP probability and \(\phi_i\) is the beta-binomial precision parameter.

title: 4  Overall model structure
text:
4.3 Expected EPP and grouping structure
The baseline component for the expected EPP probability is:
\[\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i) =
\alpha +
\mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta} +
u_{\operatorname{population}[i]} +
v_{\operatorname{species}[i]} +
w_{\operatorname{phylogeny}[i]}.\]
The grouping terms correspond to population identity, non-phylogenetic species identity, and phylogenetic species covariance:
\[u_{\operatorname{population}[i]} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\operatorname{population}}),\]
\[v_{\operatorname{species}[i]} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\operatorname{species}}),\]
\[w_{\operatorname{phylogeny}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\operatorname{phylogeny}}\mathbf{A}),\]
where \(\mathbf{A}\) is the phylogenetic correlation matrix.
Here \(\mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}\) denotes the fixed-effect part of the model. The exact predictors differ between the environmental models, but the linear predictor always combines fixed effects with the same random-effect structure: population_id, species_nonphylo, and species_phylo with the phylogenetic covariance matrix.
In brms notation, this is:
(1 | population_id) +
(1 | species_nonphylo) +
(1 | gr(species_phylo, cov = phylo_mat))

title: 4  Overall model structure
text:
4.4 Precision parameter
The parameter \(\phi_i\) is the beta-binomial precision parameter. It controls the amount of residual variation around the expected EPP probability \(\mu_i\). Lower precision corresponds to stronger extra-binomial variation among records with the same expected EPP probability. Positive coefficients in the precision component indicate higher precision and lower residual overdispersion; negative coefficients indicate lower precision and higher residual overdispersion.
In mean-only models, the precision parameter is constant across records:
\[\log(\phi_i) = \gamma_0.\]
In mean-scale models, selected predictors are also included in the precision component:
\[\log(\phi_i) =
\gamma_0 +
\mathbf{z}_i \boldsymbol{\gamma}.\]
Here \(\mathbf{z}_i \boldsymbol{\gamma}\) denotes the fixed-effect part of the scale model. Thus, mean-only models ask whether predictors explain average EPP, whereas mean-scale models additionally ask whether predictors explain variation in the precision of EPP estimates.

title: 4  Overall model structure
text:
4.5 Prior distributions
The preregistration did not specify prior distributions, so their selection was an analytical decision made for model fitting and is reported explicitly here. The mean-only models used the following priors_mu block:


Show code
priors_mu <- c(
  prior(normal(0, 2), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"),
  prior(exponential(1), class = "sd"),
  prior(exponential(1), class = "phi")
)


Equivalently, the intercept had a \(\mathcal{N}(0, 2^2)\) prior, each fixed-effect coefficient had a \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1^2)\) prior, each random-effect standard deviation had an \(\operatorname{Exponential}(1)\) prior, and the constant beta-binomial precision parameter \(\phi\) had an \(\operatorname{Exponential}(1)\) prior. The normal priors are weakly informative on the logit scale: they allow a broad range of baseline EPP probabilities and predictor effects while regularising implausibly extreme values; the exponential priors provide weak regularisation for positive scale parameters. For mean-scale models, the priors for the mean and random-effect components were unchanged, while the intercept and coefficients in the \(\log(\phi_i)\) component each received \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1^2)\) priors.

title: 4  Overall model structure
text:
4.6 Sampler settings
Models were fitted using four independent Markov chains run on four cores. Each chain used 10,000 iterations, of which the first 5,000 were warmup, leaving 20,000 post-warmup draws across chains. The Stan controls were set to adapt_delta = 0.99 and max_treedepth = 15. Model-specific random-number seeds were fixed in the fitting scripts.

title: 4  Overall model structure
text:
4.7 Posterior summaries and inferential interpretation
For each model coefficient \(\theta\), we report the posterior mean, the equal-tailed 95% credible interval defined by the 0.025 and 0.975 posterior quantiles, and the posterior probability of its direction. The output columns prob_positive and prob_negative are, respectively,
\[
\Pr(\theta > 0 \mid y)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\Pr(\theta < 0 \mid y).
\]
The probability of direction is
\[
pd = \max\{\Pr(\theta > 0 \mid y),\Pr(\theta < 0 \mid y)\}.
\]
Thus, prob_positive equals \(pd\) only when a positive coefficient is the more probable direction; for a predominantly negative coefficient, \(pd\) equals prob_negative. We use these quantities as continuous summaries of effect direction and uncertainty. We do not apply a posterior-probability, credible-interval, or conventional significance threshold to classify effects as statistically significant or non-significant. Interpretation is based jointly on effect magnitude, the 95% credible interval, and the probability of direction.
MCMC performance is assessed from split \(\widehat{R}\), bulk and tail effective sample sizes, divergent transitions, and transitions reaching the maximum tree depth. These diagnostics assess the reliability of posterior computation and are not treated as evidence for or against a biological effect.

title: 4  Overall model structure
text:
4.8 Baseline overall model
The baseline overall model uses only the common grouping structure, without environmental predictors. Its purpose is to provide the preregistered reference point for variance decomposition: the posterior variance attributable to population identity, non-phylogenetic species identity, and phylogenetic species covariance is estimated before adding environmental or methodological moderators. The same random-effect components can then be compared with those from models containing moderators to assess whether the moderators account for variation that was assigned to these grouping levels in the baseline model. The baseline model is therefore not used to test a separate intercept-only biological hypothesis.
Its expected-EPP component is:
\[\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i) =
\alpha +
u_{\operatorname{population}[i]} +
v_{\operatorname{species}[i]} +
w_{\operatorname{phylogeny}[i]}.\]
The precision component is:
\[\log(\phi_i) = \gamma_0.\]
In brms notation:


Show code
m_overall_population <- brms::brm(
  n_epp_broods | trials(n_broods_sampled) ~
    1 +
    (1 | population_id) +
    (1 | species_nonphylo) +
    (1 | gr(species_phylo, cov = phylo_mat_fit)),
  data = dat_model,
  data2 = list(phylo_mat_fit = phylo_mat_fit),
  family = brms::beta_binomial(link = "logit", link_phi = "log")
)

title: 4  Overall model structure
text:
4.9 Baseline variance decomposition
The table below reports posterior summaries for each random-intercept standard deviation, its corresponding variance on the latent logit scale, and its proportion of the summed random-intercept variance. Proportions are calculated within every posterior draw before summarisation, so their uncertainty retains the joint posterior dependence among components. The denominator contains the three grouping-level variances only; it does not include observation-level beta-binomial variation, which does not have a single constant residual variance on the latent scale.

title: 5  PCA for environmental predictors
text:
5.1 Overview
The environmental predictors combine climate, productivity, and geography. These variables describe related ecological gradients and should not be interpreted as fully independent axes of variation. We therefore use principal component analysis (PCA) to construct a small number of orthogonal predictors for the main environmental models.
The PCA is fitted to complete cases for the selected environmental-geographic variables.

title: 5  PCA for environmental predictors
text:
5.3 PCA construction
Precipitation was first transformed as log1p. Each of the six PCA inputs was then centred to a mean of zero and scaled to a standard deviation of one. The PCA was therefore performed on the correlation matrix (equivalently, on the covariance matrix of the standardised variables), so variables measured on different scales contributed comparably.
The sign of a PCA axis is arbitrary. PC1 is oriented so that higher values correspond to higher temperature loadings. PC2 is oriented so that higher values correspond to wetter and more productive environments.


Show code
library(dplyr)
library(readr)

pca_source <- dat_model_phylo %>%
  mutate(
    pca_record_id = if ("epp_row_id" %in% names(.)) {
      as.character(epp_row_id)
    } else {
      as.character(row_number())
    }
  )

pca_raw <- pca_source %>%
  transmute(
    pca_record_id = pca_record_id,
    tmp = tmp_cru_C_first_month,
    pre_log = log1p(pre_cru_mm_first_month),
    dtr = dtr_cru_C_first_month,
    ndvi = ndvi_first_month_median_30km,
    abs_latitude = abs_latitude,
    distance_to_coast = distance_to_coast_km
  ) %>%
  tidyr::drop_na()

pca_input <- pca_raw %>%
  transmute(
    pca_record_id = pca_record_id,
    tmp_z = as.numeric(scale(tmp)),
    pre_log_z = as.numeric(scale(pre_log)),
    dtr_z = as.numeric(scale(dtr)),
    ndvi_z = as.numeric(scale(ndvi)),
    abs_latitude_z = as.numeric(scale(abs_latitude)),
    distance_to_coast_z = as.numeric(scale(distance_to_coast))
  )

pca_vars <- pca_input %>%
  select(-pca_record_id)

pca <- prcomp(pca_vars, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)

pc1_direction <- ifelse(pca$rotation["tmp_z", "PC1"] < 0, -1, 1)
pc2_direction <- ifelse(sum(pca$rotation[c("pre_log_z", "ndvi_z"), "PC2"]) < 0, -1, 1)

pca$x[, "PC1"] <- pc1_direction * pca$x[, "PC1"]
pca$rotation[, "PC1"] <- pc1_direction * pca$rotation[, "PC1"]
pca$x[, "PC2"] <- pc2_direction * pca$x[, "PC2"]
pca$rotation[, "PC2"] <- pc2_direction * pca$rotation[, "PC2"]

scores <- as_tibble(pca$x[, 1:2]) %>%
  transmute(
    pca_record_id = pca_input$pca_record_id,
    PC1_thermal_geographic = PC1,
    PC2_wet_productive = PC2
  )

dat_model_with_environment_geography_pca <- pca_source %>%
  left_join(scores, by = "pca_record_id")

dat_pca <- pca_source %>%
  inner_join(scores, by = "pca_record_id")

dir.create("data/processed", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(
  dat_pca,
  "data/processed/dat_model_phylo_pca.rds"
)
saveRDS(
  dat_model_with_environment_geography_pca,
  "data/processed/dat_model_with_environment_geography_pca.rds"
)

loadings <- as.data.frame(pca$rotation) %>%
  rownames_to_column("variable") %>%
  mutate(
    PC1_thermal_geographic = PC1,
    PC2_wet_productive = PC2
  ) %>%
  select(variable, PC1_thermal_geographic, PC2_wet_productive, everything(), -PC1, -PC2)

variance_values <- pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)

variance_explained <- tibble(
  PC = paste0("PC", seq_along(pca$sdev)),
  variance_explained = variance_values,
  cumulative_variance = cumsum(variance_values)
)


The PCA was fitted to 448 complete observations from the 571-record input frame. The remaining 123 records had at least one missing value among the six PCA inputs and were not used to estimate the axes.

title: 5  PCA for environmental predictors
5  PCA for environmental predictors
text:
5.7 Interpretation
Based on the loadings, PC1 was interpreted as a thermal-geographic gradient. In this dataset, higher PC1 values correspond to warmer sites with greater diurnal temperature range, lower absolute latitude, and greater distance from the coast.






WarningPC1 cannot be attributed to a single component



The PC1 coefficient describes the combined thermal-geographic gradient and should not be interpreted as an independently identified effect of temperature, DTR, latitude, or distance from the coast. These constituents are correlated, so the data provide limited information about their mutually adjusted effects. In the D2 direct-predictor sensitivity model, the mean-temperature coefficient was 0.172 (95% CrI [-0.055, 0.406]) and the DTR coefficient was 0.124 (95% CrI [-0.062, 0.311]); both intervals included zero. Thus, the PC1 result supports inference only about the composite gradient: it does not identify which individual constituent accounts for the association. The PC1 and D2 results are therefore not contradictory; they answer different questions under strong collinearity.


Based on the loadings, PC2 was interpreted as a wet-productivity gradient after orienting the axis. In this dataset, higher PC2 values correspond to wetter sites with higher NDVI.
These two axes are used as the main environmental predictors in the beta-binomial EPP models.

title: 6  Main environmental mean models
6  Main environmental mean models
text:
The PCA models tested whether broad environmental-geographic gradients were associated with EPP.
The short-anomaly models tested whether signed recent deviations from local climatic conditions, measured relative to the five years preceding the breeding record, were associated with EPP.
The long-anomaly models tested whether signed deviations from the 1961-1989 climatic baseline were associated with EPP.

title: 6  Main environmental mean models
text:
6.2 Climate anomaly definitions
The anomaly models use the CRU value for one calendar month only: the first reported breeding-season month (climate_month) in the study year (climate_year). They do not average climate over the full breeding window. At locality \(\ell\), in study year \(y\) and first breeding month \(m\), let \(X_{\ell,y,m}\) denote either monthly mean temperature (degrees C) or monthly total precipitation (mm). The short-term baseline is the mean for the same locality and calendar month over the five years immediately preceding the study year:
\[
\bar X^{\mathrm{short}}_{\ell,y,m}
= \frac{1}{5}\sum_{k=y-5}^{y-1} X_{\ell,k,m},
\qquad
A^{\mathrm{short}}_{\ell,y,m}
= X_{\ell,y,m}-\bar X^{\mathrm{short}}_{\ell,y,m}.
\]
The long-term baseline is the mean for the same locality and calendar month over 1961–1989:
\[
\bar X^{\mathrm{long}}_{\ell,m}
= \frac{1}{29}\sum_{k=1961}^{1989} X_{\ell,k,m},
\qquad
A^{\mathrm{long}}_{\ell,y,m}
= X_{\ell,y,m}-\bar X^{\mathrm{long}}_{\ell,m}.
\]
Thus, all four modelled anomalies are signed differences, not absolute deviations. A positive temperature anomaly means that the first breeding month was warmer than its local baseline and a negative value means that it was cooler. A positive precipitation anomaly means wetter conditions and a negative value means drier conditions. The corresponding full-season variables in the dataset were constructed by the same signed subtraction across the full breeding window, but they are not used in these two primary anomaly models.
After complete-case filtering, each signed anomaly was standardized within the common 441-record model frame as
\[
A_z = \frac{A-\bar A_{\mathcal D}}{s_{\mathcal D}(A)},
\]
where \(\mathcal D\) is the main-model data frame. No absolute-value transformation was applied before or after standardization. Consequently, a positive regression coefficient represents increasing EPP as the anomaly becomes more positive (warmer or wetter relative to baseline); it does not represent an association with the magnitude of climatic departure irrespective of direction. Models using \(|A|\) would test a different hypothesis and were not fitted here, so their interpretation is not interchangeable with that of the earlier absolute-deviation analysis.
The following executable audit reconstructs every stored anomaly in the model frame from its study-year value and baseline. The presence of both negative and positive values, together with negligible reconstruction error for \(A=X-\bar X\), verifies the signed definition rather than relying on the column names.


Show code
anomaly_audit %>%
  mutate(
    max_abs_reconstruction_error = format(
      max_abs_reconstruction_error,
      scientific = TRUE,
      digits = 2
    )
  ) %>%
  rename(
    Predictor = predictor,
    `Records compared` = n_compared,
    Negative = n_negative,
    Zero = n_zero,
    Positive = n_positive,
    `Max |stored - (observed - baseline)|` = max_abs_reconstruction_error
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))

title: 6  Main environmental mean models
text:
6.8 Beta-binomial precision (\(\phi\))
The beta-binomial precision parameter quantifies residual extra-binomial heterogeneity after conditioning on the fixed effects and the three random-intercept components. Larger \(\phi\) means less extra-binomial variation, with the ordinary binomial approached as \(\phi\) increases. The corresponding within-record correlation among Bernoulli trials is \(\rho = 1/(\phi + 1)\).


Show code
if (is.na(phi_file)) {
  stop("The beta-binomial precision summaries are missing.")
}

phi_results <- read_csv_safe(phi_file) %>%

section: 7.6 Interpretation relative to the PCA model
text:
7.6 Interpretation relative to the PCA model
Mean temperature had a posterior coefficient of 0.172 on the logit scale (95% CrI [-0.055, 0.406]; probability of a positive direction = 0.932). DTR had a coefficient of 0.124 (95% CrI [-0.062, 0.311]; probability of a positive direction = 0.904). Both coefficients point in the same direction as the positive PC1 association, because higher PC1 denotes warmer sites with greater DTR, but both 95% credible intervals include zero. None of the other directly estimated environmental, geographic, or methodological coefficients had a 95% credible interval excluding zero.
On the same model frame, PC1 correlated 0.830 with temperature, 0.802 with DTR, and -0.834 with absolute latitude. The PCA coefficient therefore captures their shared thermal-geographic variation. The registered direct-predictor model does not identify whether the main PC1 association is attributable to temperature, DTR, latitude, or another constituent: separating those contributions is limited by the correlation structure rather than contradicted by the direction of the direct estimates.

title: 7  Registered direct-predictor model
section: 7.9 Prior sensitivity of the primary models
text:
7.9 Prior sensitivity of the primary models
To assess whether the primary environmental results were driven by the weakly informative fixed-effect prior, we refitted the PCA, short-anomaly, and long-anomaly mean models after replacing the common prior on non-intercept coefficients, \(\operatorname{Normal}(0,1)\), with either \(\operatorname{Normal}(0,0.5)\) or \(\operatorname{Normal}(0,2)\). Each refit used the same 441-record model frame, formula, beta-binomial family, random effects, intercept prior \(\operatorname{Normal}(0,2)\), exponential(1) priors on group-level SDs and \(\phi\), and sampler settings as its primary counterpart. Only the prior SD for class b changed; the sensitivity fits used new seeds.


Show code

prior_focal_file <- file.path(
  prior_sensitivity_dir, "focal_coefficients_prior_sensitivity.csv"
)
prior_stability_file <- file.path(
  prior_sensitivity_dir, "prior_sensitivity_stability_summary.csv"
)
prior_diagnostics_file <- file.path(
  prior_sensitivity_dir, "diagnostics_prior_sensitivity.csv"
)

if (!all(file.exists(c(
  prior_focal_file, prior_stability_file, prior_diagnostics_file
)))) {
  stop("Prior-sensitivity result files are missing.")
}

prior_focal <- read_csv_unicode(prior_focal_file)
prior_stability <- read_csv_unicode(prior_stability_file)
prior_diagnostics <- read_csv_unicode(prior_diagnostics_file)

focal_stability <- prior_stability %>%
  filter(scope == "focal environmental coefficients") %>%
  arrange(prior_sd)
all_fixed_stability <- prior_stability %>%
  filter(scope == "all non-intercept fixed effects") %>%
  arrange(prior_sd)

if (nrow(focal_stability) != 2L || nrow(all_fixed_stability) != 2L) {
  stop("Prior-sensitivity stability summaries are incomplete.")
}
if (any(prior_stability$n_interval_conclusions_changed != 0L)) {
  stop("A prior-sensitivity interval conclusion changed; update the written interpretation.")
}

The main-effects-only models had slightly higher expected predictive accuracy than their interaction counterparts (ELPD differences of 1.92 for the short anomaly and 1.51 for the long anomaly, with the main-effects model as the reference). These LOO comparisons are explicitly treated as approximate: several observations had Pareto \(k>0.7\) and each interaction fit had one observation with \(k>1\). The posterior coefficient and its uncertainty therefore remain the primary evidence for the confirmatory interaction tests.

8.9.1 Observation-level Pareto-k audit
High Pareto-k values were inspected against latitude and study intensity, rather than only counted. Across the interaction analysis, none of the problematic observations belonged to the five best-studied populations and their median population record count was one. They therefore are not an artefact of a few intensively sampled European populations. Tropical records were overrepresented: they comprise 8.4% of the full frame but 22–40% of the high-k sets, depending on the matched model. Recurring observations included Ardea ibis at absolute latitude 22.5 degrees (observed EPP proportion 0.613; maximum k 1.206) and Spheniscus humboldti at 15.37 degrees (observed EPP proportion 0). This identifies sparse, biologically unusual low-latitude records as an important source of predictive difficulty.

title: 9  Within- and between-population temperature-anomaly effects
text:
9.3 Within-population centring
Following the within-subject-centring definition of van de Pol and Wright (2009), adapted here from subjects to populations, for temperature anomaly \(x_{ij}\) in record \(i\) from population \(j\) the script constructs the population mean \(\bar{x}_j\) and the within-population departure \(x_{ij}-\bar{x}_j\). Both components use the centre and standard deviation of the original anomaly on the complete 441-row model frame:
\[
x^{between}_{ij} = \frac{\bar{x}_j - \bar{x}}{s_x}, \qquad
x^{within}_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j}{s_x}.
\]
Here, \(\bar{x}_j\) is explicitly the population mean of the temperature anomaly, not the mean of raw or baseline temperature. The source-variable audit below stops the script if a raw-temperature or baseline-temperature column is substituted. Using the same scale for both components makes the posterior contrast \(\beta_{within}-\beta_{between}\) meaningful.

The observation-level audit does not support domination by the best-studied populations: none of the observations with Pareto \(k>0.7\) came from the five largest populations, and the median record count of their populations was one. title: 10  Seasonal temperature variability
text:
10.1 Overview
To complement our analyses of local environmental conditions and year-specific climatic anomalies, we quantified within-year temperature variability following Botero and Rubenstein (2012). This descriptor represents the average variance in monthly temperatures within a year and therefore characterises persistent seasonal thermal variability at a locality rather than temporal variation among breeding seasons or a year-specific departure from local conditions. We tested its association with EPP using the same population-resolved Bayesian phylogenetic beta-binomial framework as in the primary analyses. This supplementary analysis applies an established climatic descriptor to our data and is not intended as a direct replication of the earlier species-level analysis.
The analysis addresses one question: Is population-level EPP associated with within-year temperature variability in our population-year dataset?

title: 10  Seasonal temperature variability
text:
10.2 Climate variable
Monthly mean temperature was taken from CRU TS v4.09 for the fixed 1961–1990 reference period. Each study locality was matched to the nearest valid 0.5° land cell within 100 km. No climate values were imputed. This v4.09 fit is the retained analysis used on this page, consistent with the product version used throughout the project. The earlier v4.10 fit is preserved in its original directory for auditability but is not used for inference here.
The version audit used the same assigned grid cell at all 162 localities. The v4.09 and legacy v4.10 descriptors were nearly perfectly correlated, but were not identical: 60 localities differed by more than 0.001 °C², the mean absolute difference was 0.050 °C², and the maximum was 1.103 °C². We therefore refitted the model rather than relabelling the legacy output.

Let \(T_{ym}\) be monthly mean temperature in year \(y\) and month \(m\), and let \(\bar{T}_y\) be the mean of the 12 monthly values in year \(y\). The retained descriptor is
\[
V_T = \frac{1}{30}\sum_{y=1961}^{1990}
\left[\frac{1}{11}\sum_{m=1}^{12}(T_{ym}-\bar{T}_y)^2\right].
\]
Thus, br_tmp_withinyear_var is the mean across 30 years of the sample variance among the 12 monthly temperatures within each year. Its units are °C². It measures persistent seasonal differences among months. It is not diurnal temperature range, variation among years, or a year-specific climatic anomaly. The predictor was standardised after complete-case filtering of the model frame.

title: 10  Seasonal temperature variability
text:
10.3 Statistical model
We modelled the number of EPP broods out of the number sampled with a Bayesian beta-binomial model and logit link. Standardised within-year temperature variability was the focal predictor. Nest-box use and marker type were included as methodological covariates. Random intercepts accounted for population, non-phylogenetic species identity, and phylogenetic covariance among species. The response family, priors, four-chain sampling scheme, 10,000 iterations with 5,000 warm-up iterations, and sampler controls were identical to the primary mean model. The prior block was also checked programmatically against the primary fitting script. The v4.09 refit used seed 1611 and was saved separately from the legacy v4.10 fit.


Show code
n_epp_broods | trials(n_broods_sampled) ~
  br_tmp_withinyear_var_z + nest_box + marker_type +
  (1 | population_id) + (1 | species_nonphylo) +
  (1 | gr(species_phylo, cov = phylo_mat_fit))

title: 11  Comparison with Botero & Rubenstein (2012)
11  Comparison with Botero & Rubenstein (2012)
text:
WarningScope of the comparison: context, not a formal replication



Only 44 of the 122 species in B&R’s infidelity dataset occur in the present annual-data model set. This limited overlap is driven primarily by our requirement for year-resolved population records, not by failed taxonomy: all 122 B&R names were resolved to Clements v2025. In addition, adult mortality and coloniality, which entered B&R’s candidate model, are not available consistently in our dataset. Our models instead retain the pre-specified phylogenetic, population, marker-type, and nest-box controls.
Consequently, the analyses in this chapter provide comparative context and a test of generalisability, not a formal replication of B&R’s complete analysis. The separate Table S1 check below validates the PGLS implementation on their original response and predictors; it does not remove the differences in species coverage, covariates, or phylogeny.

title: 11  Comparison with Botero & Rubenstein (2012)
text:
11.2 Climate reconstruction
Monthly CRU TS v4.09 temperature and precipitation were extracted at the audited 0.5-degree locality cells. The locality-to-cell assignments were held fixed while changing the CRU product version, so the v4.09–v4.10 comparison does not conflate product version with spatial remapping. All populations use the fixed 1961–1990 reference window, preventing the derived climate descriptors from being confounded with study year. No climate value was imputed. Sites without a reported breeding-season end month retain the two within-year metrics but are excluded from analyses requiring among-year breeding-season variance.
Breeding seasons that cross December/January are treated as one continuous season: months from the reported start through December use reference year \(y\), whereas January-side months use \(y+1\). Thus, a season beginning in 1990 may use calendar months from 1991. The v4.09 extraction consequently includes the 1991–2000 archives solely to complete the 1961–1990 reference seasons. All 23 unique cross-year locality–season combinations (63 population-year records) retained 30 complete temperature and precipitation seasons.
For variable \(x\) in year \(y\), within-year variance is \(s_y^2 = \operatorname{Var}(x_{y,1}, \ldots, x_{y,12})\); the locality value is the mean of \(s_y^2\) across 1961–1990. Among-year variance is the variance, across those 30 years, of the mean over the reported breeding-season months. The four variables are:







Variable
Definition




br_tmp_withinyear_var
Mean annual variance of the 12 monthly temperatures


br_pre_withinyear_var
Mean annual variance of the 12 monthly precipitation totals


br_tmp_amongyear_var
Variance among annual breeding-season mean temperatures


br_pre_amongyear_var
Variance among annual breeding-season mean precipitation totals



Each predictor is standardised only after complete-case filtering of its own model frame. DTR is not included in the comparison models: daily thermal amplitude and B&R’s seasonal monthly variance are different quantities.

11.4 Validation of the PGLS pipeline on B&R Table S1
Before applying the species-level PGLS workflow to our data, we tested it on the 122 original infidelity rows in B&R Table S1. The source workbook is accepted only if its SHA-256 checksum and row count match the recorded source manifest. Following the reported final infidelity model, the response is the arcsine-square-root transformation of the proportion of broods with EPP; adult mortality and within-year temperature variance are standardised; and a PGLS with Pagel’s lambda is fitted. This checksum-verified validation uses B&R’s published Table S1 values and is therefore invariant to our CRU product version; its existing validated fit is retained rather than needlessly refitted.

The reproduced temperature-seasonality coefficient is required programmatically to round to B&R’s published value of 0.042; a mismatch stops the pipeline. The original RAxML tree is available in the article package only as a plotted PDF rather than a machine-readable tree with branch lengths. We therefore use the current dated Clements tree pruned to the 122 Table S1 species. The coefficient is the primary implementation check; differences in the reproduced \(t\), \(P\), and lambda are retained in the table as transparent secondary consequences of using a different phylogeny.

title: 11  Comparison with Botero & Rubenstein (2012)
text:
11.5 Bayesian comparison models
The priors are reproduced literally from the main fitting script and compared programmatically with its parsed priors_mu assignment before fitting. A difference stops the script. All three models otherwise use the main model’s beta-binomial family, sampler settings, population random intercept, non-phylogenetic species intercept, phylogenetic covariance, nest-box effect, and marker-type effect. Coloniality and adult mortality were unavailable and were not replaced by new proxies.

11.5.1 B1: retained B&R predictor


Show code
m_br_tmp_withinyear <- brms::brm(
  brms::bf(
    n_epp_broods | trials(n_broods_sampled) ~
      br_tmp_withinyear_var_z + nest_box + marker_type +
      (1 | population_id) + (1 | species_nonphylo) +
      (1 | gr(species_phylo, cov = phylo_cov)),
    phi ~ 1
  ),
  data = dat_b1,
  data2 = list(phylo_cov = phylo_b1),
  family = brms::beta_binomial(link = "logit", link_phi = "log"),
  prior = priors_mu,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 10000, warmup = 5000,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99, max_treedepth = 15),
  seed = 2411,

)

11.5.2 B1b: retained B&R predictor adjusted for latitude

B1 provides no support for the positive B&R association: the standardised within-year temperature-variance coefficient is approximately \(-0.05\) (95% CrI \([-0.23, 0.13]\)). In B1b it remains null at approximately \(-0.02\) (\([-0.21, 0.17]\)), while absolute latitude is also unsupported at approximately \(-0.11\) (\([-0.32, 0.10]\)). Thus, adjustment for latitude does not uncover an independent seasonality effect, and neither predictor explains the other’s null association. Exact posterior summaries and diagnostics are reported in the tables above.
In B2, neither temperature coefficient is supported: within-year temperature variance is \(-0.085\) (95% CrI \([-0.296, 0.128]\)) and among-year seasonal temperature variance is \(0.026\) (\([-0.162, 0.213]\)). Within-year precipitation variance is negative at \(-0.221\) (\([-0.445, -0.001]\), probability of direction \(=0.976\)), whereas among-year seasonal precipitation variance is positive but uncertain at \(0.190\) (\([-0.014, 0.394]\), probability of direction \(=0.966\)). The former interval only narrowly excludes zero and its v4.09 estimate differs from the v4.10 estimate by \(-0.001\); the threshold crossing is therefore not a material product-version effect. With four correlated climate predictors and no backward elimination, it is treated as a weak secondary signal rather than a selected independent effect.

title: 11  Comparison with Botero & Rubenstein (2012)
section: 11.6 C1: Species-level PGLS on our data
text:
11.6 C1: Species-level PGLS on our data
To separate a methodological difference from a sampling difference, the current observations are aggregated to species means, EPP is transformed as \(\arcsin(\sqrt{p})\), the climate predictors are standardised, and a PGLS with Pagel’s \(\lambda\) is fitted. The model contains within-year temperature and precipitation variance and uses the same Clements-matched phylogeny. This is a supplementary decomposition of the discrepancy, not a preferred primary model.
